Ovoid/bullet toe fullness, height of the chevron band, number of incised triangles in the band, and the turned collar above it. Whether the foot is integral to the shaft turning or a separate glued turning is not resolvable from these views.

Front, rear and two side seat rails forming a closed rectangle; plain rectangular section in secondary wood, joints pinned with visible round pegs. Axes: length, depth of rail (this one is deep because the cover wraps over it), and whether the front edge is straight or serpentine in plan.

Horizontal rail across the back frame at roughly lumbar height, lapped past the central back post; purely a tacking ground for the inside-back cover. Axes: length, height on the back frame, count (add rails as the back gets taller).

One sawn rail carrying a double-ogee 'camel' silhouette with a central hump flanked by two lower lobes, sweeping down into the ends. Axes: number of lobes (scales with seat count), lobe amplitude, end sweep. The top-edge curve is the single most transferable spline in the object.

plan dimension, height, arris treatment (here a plain square alabaster block with a light top chamfer, ~27.8 cm square). Retargets to any pedestal, baluster, statue base or newel foot by changing footprint and height only.

lathe profile of the spreading torus, flare ratio, lappet count around the ring, bead pitch on the upper fillet. Sits on the plinth as a separate spun/cast brass shell; retargets to lamp standards, candlesticks, urn bases.

Parent assembly of the two turned spindle entries below — NOT an extra piece of stone. Total height, diameter, and the ORDER of the stacked segments are the variation axes. The whole design is a stack grammar: plinth / foot / gilt drum / jewel band / torsade drum / collar / jewel band / plain drum / jewel band / gilt drum / capital / abacus.
length, diameter, entasis (this one is very slightly tapered), and the density of the surface ornament it carries. Surface is otherwise plain lathe-turned alabaster — a bare cylinder primitive.

helix pitch, number of starts, and the alternation rule. Here a two-start helix alternating a plain rounded rope with a beaded/gadrooned rope, terminated top and bottom by a plain collar ring. Pitch and rope profile are the whole recipe; retargets to twist-turned legs, bedposts, altar columns.

register count (here 2 stacked lappet registers separated by a bead-and-reel band), drum height, and lappet instance count around the circumference. The upper and lower sleeves are the SAME part used twice — the clearest exact-reuse evidence on the object.

count: NOT DETERMINABLE
variation_axis: Plain gilt rings clamp the top and bottom edge of each jewelled band and each gilt sleeve. At least 8 are visible, but individual rings merge visually with the adjacent drum rims at every published resolution, so no honest count exists. Diameter is the only parameter; the profile is one shared half-round.

Distinct from the gilt collars: this one is cut in the STONE — three reeds above and three below a sunken jewelled register, with no metal ring at all. Reed count and register depth are the parameters. Important construction fact: it proves the jewel bands are not all metal.

The circumferential path along which cabochons and strapwork are instanced. Five occurrences: two flanking the upper gilt sleeve, one at the mid-shaft collar, two flanking the lower gilt sleeve. Variation = how many bands, where they land in the stack, and jewel spacing along the path.

count: NOT DETERMINABLE

At least 4 distinct registers, but each wraps 360 degrees and only ~half is ever visible, so no count. Variation = curve family, swag sag, repeat count.
